comparison: Perfect agreement on PPCN method (C72, C73). Both evaluations strongly support this methodological contribution, with peer reviewers calling it 'an important new bioinformatics tool' and OpenEval noting it is 'clearly defined and validated using simulated data.'

Strong agreement on core metabolic enrichment findings (C36-C39 overlap with C3, C36-C39). Both evaluations support the identification of enriched metabolic modules in IBD, with peer reviewers affirming 'strong evidence for an enrichment of bacteria with high metabolic independence' and OpenEval validating the stringent statistical approach.

Agreement on HMI population enrichment in IBD (C50-C52 overlap with C50-C53). Both evaluations support the statistical evidence for differential distribution of HMI populations, with peer reviewers noting these bacteria 'seem to be the only species that are able to survive in a stressed gut environment.'

Strong agreement on classifier performance (C3, C57-C61 overlap with C4, C57-C61). Both evaluations affirm the machine learning classifier's accuracy and robustness, with peer reviewers noting it is 'more robust to individual's lifestyles and geographic origin than previously proposed methods.'

Agreement on generalization to antibiotic stress (C4-C5, C62, C64-C66). Both evaluations support the classifier's application beyond IBD, with peer reviewers accepting this as evidence for 'a general loss in host health' and OpenEval noting independent validation from Palleja et al., 2018.

Strong agreement on overarching conclusions (C6, C67-C68). Both evaluations strongly endorse the study's main findings, with peer reviewers stating 'the implications of this study have the potential to spur a paradigm shift in the field' and OpenEval noting convergent evidence from multiple analyses.

Agreement on conceptual framework (C69-C71). Both evaluations support the 'bystander' interpretation, with peer reviewers calling it 'a magnificent contribution to the field' and OpenEval noting it is supported by data but acknowledging the hypothesis requires further testing for causality.

Agreement on dataset composition and quality control (C27-C31 overlap with C27-C32). Both evaluations accept the dataset and QC procedures, with peer reviewers noting potential limitations from public datasets but concluding 'the authors have recognised these issues and their results were robust.'

Agreement on normalization effects and validation (C33-C35 overlap with C33-C35, C47-C49). Both evaluations support the PPCN normalization approach, with peer reviewers praising 'detailed assessment of the accuracy and robustness' and OpenEval noting the reversal of trends demonstrates confounding by diversity.

Agreement on reference genome analysis (C74-C82). Both evaluations accept the HMI classification approach and its limitations, with peer reviewers noting 'limitations are clearly addressed throughout the manuscript' and OpenEval acknowledging the arbitrary threshold but validating the approach through consistent enrichment patterns.

Agreement on amino acid biosynthesis findings (C40-C41). Both evaluations accept the discrepancy with earlier studies and alignment with recent work, with peer reviewers accepting this as part of the overall metabolic enrichment pattern and OpenEval noting methodological improvements may explain differences.

Agreement on metabolic network properties (C42-C44 overlap with C42-C45). Both evaluations support the interconnectedness findings, with peer reviewers treating these as supporting details for the HMI concept and OpenEval noting the quantitative analysis suggests coordinated metabolic capabilities.

Agreement on cobalamin biosynthesis example (C55-C56). Both evaluations accept this as supporting the cross-feeding disruption interpretation, with peer reviewers treating it as illustrative detail and OpenEval noting it provides specific mechanistic support for the hypothesis.

Agreement on validation against selection bias (C89-C90). Both evaluations praise the repeated sample-split analysis, with peer reviewers noting 'extensive benchmarking and validation' and OpenEval stating it provides 'strong evidence for the stability and validity of the identified modules.'

Agreement on acknowledged limitations (C83-C84). Both evaluations view the authors' acknowledgment of limitations positively, with peer reviewers stating 'limitations are clearly addressed' and 'unlikely to have affected the conclusions,' and OpenEval noting this 'strengthens the overall credibility of the work.'

Agreement on comparison with previous work (C85-C88). Both evaluations accept the critique of previous classifier approaches, with peer reviewers endorsing the claim that the function-based index is 'more robust' than taxonomy-based methods, and OpenEval noting the critique is 'fair and well-supported by citations.'

Agreement on background claims (C1-C2 overlap with broader background set). Both evaluations accept the background framing, with peer reviewers implicitly accepting these as appropriate context and OpenEval noting they represent 'established scientific consensus' and 'genuine knowledge gap.'

Agreement on diversity patterns (C32). Both evaluations support this validation finding, with peer reviewers accepting dataset quality and OpenEval noting alignment with previous literature and validation of the dataset.

Agreement on batch effect analysis (C47). Both evaluations accept the per-cohort analysis as addressing potential biases, with peer reviewers noting results were 'robust to analyses performed at a per-cohort basis' and OpenEval stating this 'strengthens confidence in the biological signal.'

Subtle difference in emphasis on functional annotation bias (C48-C49). OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN, noting the authors 'cannot definitively determine the source or full implications' and calling it 'an important limitation.' Peer reviewers implicitly accepted this as part of the overall validation without specific concern, treating acknowledged limitations as appropriately handled.
